fedFunds.unit: percent per annum (annual average of monthly averages)
fedFunds.source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System via FRED, series FEDFUNDS (Federal Funds Effective Rate, monthly, not seasonally adjusted), https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=FEDFUNDS, retrieved 2026-10-22 (FRED last updated 2026-10-01).
fedFunds.note: Annual values computed by us as the simple mean of the 12 monthly values (rounded half-up to 2 decimals); they match FRED's own annual-average aggregation (fq=Annual&fam=avg) for every year 1955-2025. 2026 = mean of the 9 months available, January-September 2026 (Jan-Apr 3.64, May-Aug 3.63, Sep 3.75). For context (not included in the 2026 value): the daily effective rate (FRED DFF) stepped from 3.63% to 3.88% on 2026-09-17 and was 3.88% on every day of 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-20.

mortgage30.unit: percent per annum (annual average of weekly survey rates)
mortgage30.source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey via FRED, series MORTGAGE30US (30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States, weekly, not seasonally adjusted), https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=MORTGAGE30US, retrieved 2026-10-22 (FRED last updated 2026-10-22).
mortgage30.note: Series is weekly, so annual values were computed by us as the simple mean of all weekly observations dated in each calendar year (rounded half-up to 2 decimals); this matches FRED's annual-average aggregation exactly for 1972-2026. 2026 = mean of the 42 weekly readings from 2026-01-08 through 2026-10-22 (latest reading 7.32% on 2026-10-22; 7.40% on 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-15).

treasury10.unit: percent per annum (annual average of monthly averages)
treasury10.source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15) via FRED, series GS10 (Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 10-Year Constant Maturity, monthly, not seasonally adjusted), https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=GS10, retrieved 2026-10-22 (FRED last updated 2026-10-01).
treasury10.note: Annual values computed by us as the simple mean of the 12 monthly values (rounded half-up to 2 decimals); they match FRED's annual-average aggregation for every year 1954-2025. 2026 = mean of the 9 months available, January-September 2026 (September 2026 = 4.99). For context (not included in the 2026 value): the daily series DGS10 averaged 5.21% over the 13 trading days 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-20.

tariffs.unit: values = average effective tariff rate, percent (customs duties / goods imports x 100); customsDuties and goodsImports in billions of current US dollars
tariffs.source: BEA National Income and Product Accounts via FRED: customs duties = B235RC1A027NBEA (annual, 1947-2025) and B235RC1Q027SBEA (quarterly SAAR, used for 2026); goods imports = A255RC1A027NBEA (annual) and A255RC1Q027SBEA (quarterly SAAR, used for 2026). https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=B235RC1A027NBEA ; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=A255RC1A027NBEA ; retrieved 2026-10-22 (FRED last updated 2026-09-30).
tariffs.note: CALENDAR years, NIPA (accrual) basis. Effective rate computed by us = duties / goods imports. The annual NIPA series match the average of the quarterly SAAR values to within rounding in every year 1959-2025 (checked). 2026 = average of the two quarters available (Q1 326.223 and Q2 306.398 SAAR for duties; Q1 3439.879 and Q2 3727.887 SAAR for goods imports), i.e., an annualized first-half rate. IMPORTANT for 2025-2026: on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs; BEA records the resulting refunds (about $166 billion excluding interest) as a capital transfer from the federal government in 2026Q1, NOT as a reduction of customs duties (BEA FAQ 1488, https://www.bea.gov/help/faq/1488), so the NIPA duties here are gross of refunds. Cash collections net of refunds are in treasuryMTS below. USITC calendar-year ratio of calculated duties to imports for consumption (the classic historical series) is in usitcRatio for 1947-2010 as a cross-check.

quarterlyRecent.unit: [quarter start date, customs duties $B SAAR, goods imports $B SAAR, effective rate %]
quarterlyRecent.source: FRED B235RC1Q027SBEA and A255RC1Q027SBEA (BEA NIPA), retrieved 2026-10-22.

usitcRatio.unit: [year, calculated duties $B, imports for consumption $B, duties as % of total imports, duties as % of dutiable imports]
usitcRatio.source: U.S. International Trade Commission, Statistical Services Division, "Value of U.S. Imports for Consumption, Duties Collected, and Ratio of Duties to Values, 1891-2010" (March 2011), read from the UNT Libraries web archive copy of dataweb.usitc.gov/scripts/AVE.PDF: https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/web/20130213204908mp_/http://dataweb.usitc.gov/scripts/AVE.PDF
usitcRatio.note: Calendar years 1940 onward; values converted from $1,000 to $B by us; ratio columns as printed by USITC (match our recomputation). A newer edition covering 1891-2024 exists at usitc.gov/documents/dataweb/ave_table.pdf (Feb 2025) but returned HTTP 403 to our fetcher, so 2011-2024 are not included here (null).

treasuryMTS.unit: billions of US dollars; customs duties receipts, cash basis
treasuryMTS.source: U.S. Treasury, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 4 (Receipts), line "Customs Duties", via Fiscal Data API https://api.fiscaldata.treasury.gov/services/api/fiscal_service/v1/accounting/mts/mts_table_4 (filter classification_desc = Customs Duties), retrieved 2026-10-22; latest month September 2026. Monthly goods imports: Census Bureau, U.S. Imports of Goods by Customs Basis from World, seasonally adjusted (FRED IMP0004, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=IMP0004, last updated 2026-10-06, latest month August 2026).
treasuryMTS.note: Fiscal year = Oct-Sep. Gross = gross receipts; refunds = customs refunds paid; net = gross - refunds. The surge in refunds from May 2026 (net receipts negative in May, June and July 2026) follows the 2026-02-20 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling. grossDutiesPctPriorMonthImports is our approximate monthly effective rate = gross customs duties received in month t / Census-basis goods imports (SA) in month t-1, lagged one month because most duties are paid on a monthly statement the month after entry; it mixes NSA receipts with SA imports, so read it as approximate. Net-receipt ratios are not shown because 2026 refunds relate to earlier imports.

calendarYear.note: Sums of monthly values computed by us; 2026 covers January-September only (9 months). The API series starts in March 2015, so CY2015 is omitted.

context.supremeCourt: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (decided 2026-02-20, 6-3): IEEPA does not authorize tariffs; the reciprocal and fentanyl-related IEEPA tariffs were invalidated. Sources: https://www.faegredrinker.com/en/insights/publications/2026/2/supreme-court-decides-learning-resources-inc-v-trump-and-trump-v-vos-selections-inc ; https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en-us/help/onesource-global-trade/regulatory-insights/2026/february-20th/supreme-court-rejects-ieepa-as-a-tariff-statute
context.beaRefundTreatment: BEA FAQ 1488 (published 2026-04-30, modified 2026-06-25): IEEPA refunds of about $166 billion excluding interest ($664 billion at an annual rate) are classified as a capital transfer from the federal government, recorded in 2026Q1 on an accrual basis; they do not affect GDP. https://www.bea.gov/help/faq/1488
context.yaleBudgetLabStatutoryRate: Yale Budget Lab, The State of U.S. Tariffs (published 2026-07-24): as of July 24, 2026 the average statutory tariff rate was 11.1%, after Section 122 tariffs expired and were replaced by Section 301 tariffs; projected 11.8% by end-2026 under current law. This is a statutory (import-weighted applied) rate, not duties collected / imports. https://budgetlab.yale.edu/research/state-us-tariffs (PDF snapshot https://budgetlab.yale.edu/sites/default/files/page_to_pdf/1568/publication_1568.pdf)

tradeShare.source: BEA NIPA Table 1.1.10 via FRED: B020RE1A156NBEA (Shares of GDP: Exports of goods and services) and B021RE1A156NBEA (Shares of GDP: Imports of goods and services), annual; totals from EXPGSA, IMPGSA and GDPA (nominal $B). https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=B020RE1A156NBEA ; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=B021RE1A156NBEA ; retrieved 2026-10-22.
tradeShare.note: values = (exports + imports) / GDP x 100, computed by us from nominal EXPGSA, IMPGSA, GDPA and rounded to 1 decimal; exports and imports arrays are the official BEA share series (1 decimal). We recomputed both shares from the nominal series and they match the official series in all 79 years. 2026 is not included; for reference, Q1-Q2 2026 SAAR averages give exports 11.39% and imports 14.03% of GDP (computed from FRED EXPGS, IMPGS, GDP).

mobility.note: Part B benchmarks for checking a simulated population. Matrices are lists of rows (origin quintile, bottom first) with destination-quintile shares in percent. Every number was read in the cited primary document by us or our research agents; most key cells were re-checked by us against the document text (Treasury 2007 Tables 1, 2, 4, 6, 7; Chetty et al. 2014 Table II; Pew 2012 Figure 3; Hungerford CRS Table 2; Census P70-142 Figure 2; Auten-Gee-Turner NTJ 2013 Tables 1 and 5; Davis-von Wachter abstract and Tables 1-2; GAO-12-699 Table 19; Bane-Ellwood WP Table 3; Edwards 2015 Table 7; SHED 2024/2025; Bhutta-Dettling 2018; FEDS 2021-076; CFPB 2024). Single-checked items are flagged in their notes (Auten & Gee 2009 matrices; Dobkin et al. published-table values beyond those corroborated; Peterson 1996 and Jacobson-LaLonde-Sullivan 1993 from abstracts). Gaps: SHED has no 6-month measure; the AER P&P version of Auten, Gee & Turner (2013) was paywalled (its NTJ companion is used); no matrix here covers exactly 10 years with an identical definition across sources, so compare like with like (tax units pre-tax vs survey families after-tax and size-adjusted give very different bottom-quintile persistence).

treasury2007Table1.years: 1996 -> 2005 (9-year span, often described as a decade)
treasury2007Table1.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury (Nov 13, 2007; revised March 2008), "Income Mobility in the U.S. from 1996 to 2005," https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/131/Report-Income-Mobility-2008.pdf (Table 1, p.7).
treasury2007Table1.note: Non-dependent primary and secondary taxpayers age 25+ in 1996 who filed in both years (~96,700 returns, 169,300 taxpayers in the panel, representing 117.1M taxpayers); pre-tax cash income incl. realized capital gains, 2005 dollars, not size-adjusted. Quintiles defined relative to the full age-25+ filing population each year, so the panel's 2005 column shares are 13.2/16.8/19.6/23.3/27.1% rather than 20% each (aging panel vs. young entrants). Key cells: 57.6% of the bottom quintile moved up (report rounds to 58%); 5.3% reached the top quintile; 69.4% of the top quintile stayed; 42.6% of the top 1% stayed in the top 1%.

treasury2007Table2.cols: 2005 income quintile (ranked within the panel only, so each column = 20%)
treasury2007Table2.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury (Nov 13, 2007; revised March 2008), "Income Mobility in the U.S. from 1996 to 2005," https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/131/Report-Income-Mobility-2008.pdf (Table 2, p.9).
treasury2007Table2.note: Same panel as Table 1 but quintiles defined within the panel, which is the closer analogue to a closed simulated population. 44.9% of the bottom quintile moved up (report: 45%); 61.4% of the top quintile stayed; 40.3% of the top 1% stayed.

treasury2007Top001.unit: percent of the top 0.01% of 1996 who were still in the top 0.01% in 2005
treasury2007Top001.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury (Nov 13, 2007; revised March 2008), "Income Mobility in the U.S. from 1996 to 2005," https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/131/Report-Income-Mobility-2008.pdf (Table 4, p.11; summary p.2).
treasury2007Top001.note: Summary: only 25 percent of the top 1/100 of 1 percent remained in that group. Their median real income fell 64.6% (Table 6); median real income of the 1996 top 1% fell 25.8% (Table 3), while median income of all panel taxpayers rose 24.2%.

treasury2007HouseholdDecades.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury (Nov 13, 2007; revised March 2008), "Income Mobility in the U.S. from 1996 to 2005," https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/131/Report-Income-Mobility-2008.pdf (Table 7, p.14).
treasury2007HouseholdDecades.note: Household sample following the primary taxpayer; the report concludes mobility was essentially unchanged between the two decades.

autenGee2009.cols: end-year income quintile (relative to total age-25+ population)
autenGee2009.source: Auten & Gee (2009), "Income Mobility in the United States: New Evidence from Income Tax Data," National Tax Journal 62(2): 301-328 (Table 2 p.307; Table 6 p.313; Table 5 p.312). DOI 10.17310/ntj.2009.2.05.
autenGee2009.note: Income divided by sqrt(household size); ~107,000 returns / 175,800 taxpayers age 25+ in 1996. VERIFICATION: read by our research agent from an archived copy of the publisher PDF (web.archive.org of ntanet.org; live link 404); we could not re-open it ourselves, so treat as single-checked. Within-panel ranking (Table 3): bottom stays 57.7%, bottom->top 3.0%, top stays 59.8%, top 1% stays 38.5%. Share changing quintile: 58.3% (1987-96) vs 57.5% (1996-2005).

autenGeeTurner2013.years: top-1% persistence: base years 2000-2005, five-year windows; 20-year mobility: 1987 -> 2007
autenGeeTurner2013.source: Auten, Gee & Turner (2013), "New Perspectives on Income Mobility and Inequality," National Tax Journal 66(4): 893-912 (Table 1 p.897, Table 4 p.900, Table 5 p.902), read at https://tyap.net/mediaf/auten,_gee,_turner_.pdf ; companion to Auten, Gee & Turner (2013), "Income Inequality, Mobility, and Turnover at the Top in the US, 1987-2010," AER Papers & Proceedings 103(3): 168-172 (abstract checked at https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/aecrev/v103y2013i3p168-72.html).
autenGeeTurner2013.note: Top-1% persistence among taxpayers 25+: 53% (2000) to 61-63% (2002-2005) are still in the top 1% one year later, 41-49% are there five years later, 23-31% are there in every one of the six years. 20-year cells compare taxpayers 35-40 in 1987 with their age peers (55-60) in 2007; dependents 15-18 in 1987 are ranked by their parents' return. The AER P&P abstract (we could not read its tables) states about half of 35-40-year-olds in the top or bottom quintile in 1987 were still there in 2007 and about 30% of bottom-quintile dependents were in the bottom 20 years later.

psidHungerford1980s.source: Hungerford, CRS Report RL34434, "Income Inequality, Income Mobility, and Economic Policy: U.S. Trends in the 1980s and 1990s" (Apr 4, 2008), Table 2 panel A, p.CRS-10, https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/20080404_RL34434_be64d1aab381920155131bf341304806355ba3b7.pdf
psidHungerford1980s.note: PSID individuals; family income after taxes and transfers (incl. food stamps, excl. realized capital gains), equivalence-scale adjusted. Immobility ratio 0.377 (37.7% in the same quintile).

psidHungerford1990s.source: Hungerford, CRS Report RL34434 (2008), Table 2 panel B, p.CRS-10 (same URL as psidHungerford1980s).
psidHungerford1990s.note: Same definitions; 40.6% stayed in the same quintile. Survey-based, size-adjusted, after-tax family income shows much more bottom stickiness (53%) than tax-unit pre-tax income (Treasury 42%).

sippCensus2009to2012.source: U.S. Census Bureau, P70-142, "Dynamics of Economic Well-Being: Fluctuations in the U.S. Income Distribution: 2009-2012" (July 2017), Figure 2 p.4 and Table 1 p.5, https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2017/demo/p70-142.pdf
sippCensus2009to2012.note: SIPP 2008 panel, 113.3M households, annual household income (2012 dollars, not size-adjusted). 57.1% of households stayed in the same quintile. Short-horizon benchmark (3 years), not a decade.

psidBradbury2011.source: Bradbury (2011), "Trends in U.S. Family Income Mobility, 1969-2006," Federal Reserve Bank of Boston Working Paper 11-10, Table 2 p.38, https://www.bostonfed.org/-/media/Documents/Workingpapers/PDF/economic/wp/wp2011/wp1110.pdf
psidBradbury2011.note: PSID family heads and spouses aged 16-62; family income after taxes and transfers / sqrt(family size), two-year averages at each end. Implies 58.1% stayed in the bottom and 55.0% stayed in the top over 1995-2005.

psidAcsZimmerman2008.unit: percent of those starting in the bottom quintile, by end quintile (bottom..top)
psidAcsZimmerman2008.source: Acs & Zimmerman (2008), "U.S. Intragenerational Economic Mobility from 1984 to 2004: Trends and Implications," Pew Economic Mobility Project, Figures 1 and 3, https://data.issuelab.org/resources/11538/11538.pdf
psidAcsZimmerman2008.note: PSID adults 25-44 at start who were heads/partners in both years; pre-tax family income incl. transfers, size-adjusted; excludes incomes under $1,200 or in the top 1%.

chetty2014RankRankSlope.years: children born 1980-82 (9,867,736 children); parent family income averaged 1996-2000 (child ~15-20); child family income averaged 2011-12 (child ~30)
chetty2014RankRankSlope.source: Chetty, Hendren, Kline & Saez (2014), "Where is the Land of Opportunity? The Geography of Intergenerational Mobility in the United States," Quarterly Journal of Economics 129(4): 1553-1623. Read: NBER WP 19843 https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w19843/w19843.pdf and authors' QJE version https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/mobility_geo.pdf (Table I, row 4).
chetty2014RankRankSlope.note: A 1 percentile increase in parent rank raises the child's expected rank by 0.341 percentiles (s.e. 0.0003). 0.323 for the 1980-85 cohorts. Pre-tax family income from tax records (AGI + tax-exempt interest + non-taxable Social Security/disability; W-2 wages + UI + SS for non-filers).

chetty2014IGE.source: Chetty, Hendren, Kline & Saez (2014), "Where is the Land of Opportunity? The Geography of Intergenerational Mobility in the United States," Quarterly Journal of Economics 129(4): 1553-1623. Read: NBER WP 19843 https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w19843/w19843.pdf and authors' QJE version https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/mobility_geo.pdf (Table I, row 1; text p.13 of WP).
chetty2014IGE.note: Log-log intergenerational income elasticity excluding children with zero income. 0.452 when parents are restricted to the 10th-90th percentiles; the paper reports a range of roughly 0.26-0.70 across specifications. The rank-rank slope is the paper's preferred, more stable measure.

chetty2014BottomToTopQuintile.unit: percent of children with bottom-quintile parents who reach the top quintile
chetty2014BottomToTopQuintile.source: Chetty, Hendren, Kline & Saez (2014), "Where is the Land of Opportunity? The Geography of Intergenerational Mobility in the United States," Quarterly Journal of Economics 129(4): 1553-1623. Read: NBER WP 19843 https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w19843/w19843.pdf and authors' QJE version https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/mobility_geo.pdf (Table II and text).
chetty2014BottomToTopQuintile.note: Compared in the paper with 11.7% in Denmark and 13.4% in Canada. 7.8% for the 1980-85 cohorts (Online Appendix Table VI). Ranges across commuting zones from 4.4% (Charlotte) to 12.9% (San Jose).

chetty2014TransitionMatrix.years: children born 1980-82; parent income 1996-2000; child income 2011-12
chetty2014TransitionMatrix.source: Chetty, Hendren, Kline & Saez (2014), "Where is the Land of Opportunity? The Geography of Intergenerational Mobility in the United States," Quarterly Journal of Economics 129(4): 1553-1623. Read: NBER WP 19843 https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w19843/w19843.pdf and authors' QJE version https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/mobility_geo.pdf (Table II).
chetty2014TransitionMatrix.note: Transposed by us from the printed table (which has parent quintiles as columns); values verified against the NBER WP 19843 text. Key cells: bottom stays bottom 33.7%; bottom to top 7.5%; top stays top 36.5%; top falls to bottom 10.9%.

chettyEtAl2014Trend.years: birth cohorts 1971-1993 (slope; 1983-93 forecast); bottom-to-top probabilities with child income measured at age 26
chettyEtAl2014Trend.source: Chetty, Hendren, Kline, Saez & Turner (2014), "Is the United States Still a Land of Opportunity? Recent Trends in Intergenerational Mobility," American Economic Review Papers & Proceedings 104(5): 141-147; read NBER WP 19844 https://rajchetty.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/mobility_trends.pdf and AER appendix https://www.aeaweb.org/articles/materials/2911
chettyEtAl2014Trend.note: Rank-rank slope roughly flat around 0.30 across 1971-1993 cohorts (fitted trend -0.0006 per year). Bottom-to-top quintile 8.4% (1971 cohort, SOI sample) vs 9.0% (1986 cohort, population sample), income at age 26. Annual cohort values: AER P&P appendix Tables 1 and 4.

pew2012TransitionMatrix.rows: parents' family-income quintile, bottom to top
pew2012TransitionMatrix.cols: adult child's family-income quintile, bottom to top
pew2012TransitionMatrix.unit: percent of row (rows sum to 100 +/- 1 from rounding)
pew2012TransitionMatrix.years: PSID children aged 0-18 in 1968 (N=2,736); parent income averaged 1967-71; child income averaged 2000-2008 (5 survey years, average age 45)
pew2012TransitionMatrix.source: Pew Charitable Trusts Economic Mobility Project (July 2012), "Pursuing the American Dream: Economic Mobility Across Generations," https://www.pew.org/~/media/legacy/uploadedfiles/pcs_assets/2012/pursuingamericandreampdf.pdf (Figure 3, p.6; appendix pp.28-30).
pew2012TransitionMatrix.note: Family income adjusted for family size (divided by sqrt of family size), 2008 dollars. Cells read from Figure 3 data labels (the report prints no table); we checked the labels in the PDF text, and they match the text figures.

pew2012Stickiness.source: Pew Charitable Trusts Economic Mobility Project (July 2012), "Pursuing the American Dream: Economic Mobility Across Generations," https://www.pew.org/~/media/legacy/uploadedfiles/pcs_assets/2012/pursuingamericandreampdf.pdf (pp.2, 4, 6).
pew2012Stickiness.note: "Stickiness at the ends": 43% raised in the bottom quintile stay there and 70% stay below the middle; 40% raised at the top stay there and 63% stay above the middle; only 4% go bottom to top. Absolute mobility: 84% have higher (family-size-adjusted) family income than their parents (93% of those raised in the bottom quintile, 70% of those raised in the top).

chetty2017AbsoluteMobility.unit: percent of children with higher real pre-tax household income at ~30 than their parents had at a similar age
chetty2017AbsoluteMobility.source: Chetty, Grusky, Hell, Hendren, Manduca & Narang (2017), "The Fading American Dream: Trends in Absolute Income Mobility Since 1940," Science 356(6336): 398-406; read NBER WP 22910 https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/abs_mobility_paper.pdf
chetty2017AbsoluteMobility.note: Benchmark (copula-stability) estimate: 92% of the 1940 birth cohort vs 50% of the 1984 cohort earn more than their parents; 1940 bounds 84-98% across plausible copulas (1984 bounds 14-88%). Science abstract: roughly 90% for 1940 vs 50% for the 1980s.

jobDisplacement.source: Davis & von Wachter (2011), "Recessions and the Costs of Job Loss," Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Fall 2011: 1-72 (abstract; Table 1 p.22; text p.17), https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2011/09/2011b_bpea_davis.pdf
jobDisplacement.note: Men aged 50 or younger with 3+ years of tenure displaced in mass layoffs at firms with 50+ employees, vs. non-displaced controls. Present value of lost earnings over 20 years at a 5% discount rate, in years of pre-displacement earnings. Abstract: losses average 1.4 years if displaced when national unemployment is below 6%, 2.8 years when above 8%. Earnings 39% (recession) / 25% (expansion) below controls in year 1, still 15-20% (recession) / ~10% (expansion) below 10-20 years out. Women aged 21-50 with 3+ years tenure: 1.5 years overall (Table 2).

jobDisplacementJLS1993.years: Pennsylvania administrative earnings data (setting as described by Davis & von Wachter 2011)
jobDisplacementJLS1993.source: Jacobson, LaLonde & Sullivan (1993), "Earnings Losses of Displaced Workers," American Economic Review 83(4): 685-709 (abstract, https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/aecrev/v83y1993i4p685-709.html).
jobDisplacementJLS1993.note: High-tenure workers separating from distressed firms suffer long-term losses averaging about 25% per year (abstract only read).

divorce.years: Health and Retirement Study 1992-2010; divorces/separations after age 50 (people born before 1954)
divorce.source: U.S. GAO (July 2012), GAO-12-699, "Retirement Security: Women Still Face Challenges," p.28 and Table 19 p.84, https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-12-699.pdf
divorce.note: Fixed-effects estimates of the change associated with divorce. Unadjusted household income: women -41%, men -23% ("nearly twice that of men's"). Adjusted for household size (per member): women -31%, men -9%. Older-adult sample, so a lower bound on child-support/custody effects at younger ages.

divorceStandardOfLiving.years: Weitzman's 1977-78 Los Angeles County divorce sample, re-analyzed
divorceStandardOfLiving.source: Peterson (1996), "A Re-Evaluation of the Economic Consequences of Divorce," American Sociological Review 61(3), article beginning p.528 (abstract via https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.2307/2096363).
divorceStandardOfLiving.note: Corrects Weitzman's widely cited -73% (women) / +42% (men) to -27% / +10% in standard of living (income relative to needs) a year after divorce. Abstract only read by our research agent.

divorceChildren.source: Tach & Eads (2014), "The cost of breaking up," IRP Focus 30(2), pp.16 and 18 cited, https://www.irp.wisc.edu/wp/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/foc302e.pdf
divorceChildren.note: Children's size-adjusted household income fell about 35% immediately after a parental divorce in both decades; net loss one year later about 30% (1980s) and about 20% (2000s). The article also summarizes earlier studies putting the drop in women's household income a year after divorce at 23-40%.

healthShock.years: HRS 1992-2012 (insured adults hospitalized at ages 50-59); California hospital discharge records 2003-2007 linked to credit reports 2002-2011 (ages 25-64)
healthShock.source: Dobkin, Finkelstein, Kluender & Notowidigdo (2018), "The Economic Consequences of Hospital Admissions," American Economic Review 108(2): 308-352 (Table 2 p.323; pp.311, 333, 336), https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/114039
healthShock.note: Earnings fall about 20% of the pre-admission mean ($45,327) on average over three years and the decline appears persistent; only ~10% of the earnings loss is replaced by social insurance. Bankruptcy rises 0.4 pp four years after admission for the insured (~33% of the 1.2% annual baseline) vs 1.4 pp for the uninsured; per the abstract, hospital admissions account for under 5% of bankruptcies in the sample. Earnings/employment figures verified against the published table by our research agent and corroborated by UC Santa Cruz news (https://news.ucsc.edu/2018/02/dobkin-hospitalization/); bankruptcy figures also appear in the 2016 working-paper version (IPR WP-16-24).

povertyEntriesBaneEllwood.unit: percent of poverty spell beginnings (each spell assigned one primary reason; household-composition changes take priority)
povertyEntriesBaneEllwood.years: PSID, non-elderly persons, spells beginning 1970-1978 (1983 working-paper version)
povertyEntriesBaneEllwood.source: Bane & Ellwood (1983), NBER Working Paper 1199, Table 3 p.21, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w1199/w1199.pdf ; published as "Slipping into and out of Poverty: The Dynamics of Spells," Journal of Human Resources 21(1): 1-23 (1986).
povertyEntriesBaneEllwood.note: Earnings declines of any household member ~50% of beginnings; transitions to a female-headed family ~11%. The 1986 published figures, as cited by McKernan & Ratcliffe (2002, p.10): head's earnings fell 37.9%, wives'/others' earnings 11.4% (all earnings 49.3%), female headship 11.1%, young adult sets up own household 14.7%, child born 8.6%. For female-headed families with children, the switch to female headship dominates (65% of beginnings in the WP text).

povertyEntriesMcKernanRatcliffe.unit: percent of poverty entrants experiencing each event (events can overlap)
povertyEntriesMcKernanRatcliffe.source: McKernan & Ratcliffe (Sept 2002), "Transition Events in the Dynamics of Poverty," Urban Institute report for HHS/ASPE, https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/migrated_legacy_files//40001/full-report.pdf ; journal version: "Events that Trigger Poverty Entries and Exits," Social Science Quarterly 86(s1): 1146-1169 (2005).
povertyEntriesMcKernanRatcliffe.note: A shift to a female-headed household carries the highest entry rate but is rare, so job loss accounts for far more entries.

povertyEntriesCensusSIPP.unit: percent of monthly poverty-spell entries preceded by each event (overlapping)
povertyEntriesCensusSIPP.source: Edwards (2015), "Crisis, Chronic, and Churning: an Analysis of Varying Poverty Experiences," U.S. Census Bureau SEHSD Working Paper 2015-06, text p.10 and appendix Table 7, https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/working-papers/2015/demo/SEHSD-WP2015-06.pdf
povertyEntriesCensusSIPP.note: "79.0 percent of all poverty entries follow declines in family earned income." Family-structure events precede only a few percent of monthly entries. Monthly SIPP and annual PSID shares are not directly comparable.

shed400Cash.years: SHED surveys fielded October 2024 (n=12,295) and October 2025 (n=12,934)
shed400Cash.source: Federal Reserve Board, "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024" (May 2025), Savings and Investments section, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2024-savings-and-investments.htm ; Federal Reserve Board, "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" (May 2026), Savings and Investments section, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-savings-investments.htm
shed400Cash.note: Share who would cover a hypothetical $400 emergency expense exclusively using cash or its equivalent (cash, savings, or a credit card paid off at the next statement). Unchanged at 63% in 2022-2025 (peak 68% in 2021). Share unable to pay the $400 by any means: 13% (2024), 12% (2025).

shed3MonthEmergencyFund.source: Federal Reserve Board, "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024" (May 2025), Savings and Investments section, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2024-savings-and-investments.htm ; Federal Reserve Board, "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" (May 2026), Savings and Investments section, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-savings-investments.htm
shed3MonthEmergencyFund.note: Q: "Have you set aside emergency or rainy day funds that would cover your expenses for 3 months in case of sickness, job loss, economic downturn, or other emergencies?" Yes: 55% in both years (54% in 2023).

shed3MonthAnyMeans.source: Federal Reserve Board, "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024" (May 2025), Savings and Investments section, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2024-savings-and-investments.htm ; Federal Reserve Board, "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" (May 2026), Savings and Investments section, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-savings-investments.htm
shed3MonthAnyMeans.note: Derived: 30% said they could not cover three months of expenses by any means (borrowing, savings, selling assets), so ~70% could (55% with a rainy-day fund + ~15% via borrowing/selling assets/other savings).

sixMonthCoverage.years: SCF 2016; SCF 2016+2019 pooled; CFPB January 2024; SHED 2024-2025 (no such question)
sixMonthCoverage.source: See scfLiquidSavings2016 (Bhutta & Dettling 2018 FEDS Note), scfLiquidSavings2016and2019 (FEDS 2021-076) and cfpbCoverageAnyMeans2024 (CFPB Making Ends Meet 2024); SHED reports: https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2024-savings-and-investments.htm and https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-savings-investments.htm
sixMonthCoverage.note: SHED has no 6-month question (checked the 2024 and 2025 reports and questionnaires), so shed = null. The SCF "Changes in U.S. Family Finances" bulletins (2019, 2022, 2025 data) do not publish a months-of-coverage share; the SCF-based 6-month figures come from Fed staff papers with different liquid-asset definitions (28% vs 39%). CFPB counts any means (borrowing, savings, selling assets, help from family).

scfLiquidSavings2016.source: Bhutta & Dettling (Nov 19, 2018), "Money in the Bank? Assessing Families' Liquid Savings using the Survey of Consumer Finances," FEDS Notes, https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/assessing-families-liquid-savings-using-the-survey-of-consumer-finances-20181119.htm
scfLiquidSavings2016.note: Liquid savings = transaction accounts, cash, prepaid cards, directly held stocks/bonds/mutual funds (excludes retirement accounts, CDs, savings bonds). Expenses = recurring monthly expenses (housing, vehicle and debt payments, food reported; utilities, insurance, health etc. imputed). By income quartile the 3-month share is 17/31/43/68% (research agent).

scfLiquidSavings2016and2019.source: Bhutta, Blair & Dettling (2021), "The Smart Money is in Cash? Financial Literacy and Liquid Savings Among U.S. Families," FEDS 2021-076, https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2021076pap.pdf
scfLiquidSavings2016and2019.note: Broader liquid-asset definition than the 2018 note (adds e.g. money market accounts) and "normal, recurring expenses"; hence higher shares than 40%/28%.

cfpbCoverageAnyMeans2024.unit: percent of households (consumers with credit records)
cfpbCoverageAnyMeans2024.source: CFPB (Nov 2024), "Making Ends Meet in 2024," Figure 3 and Table 6, pp.17-18, https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_making-ends-meet_2024-11.pdf
cfpbCoverageAnyMeans2024.note: Q: if the household lost its main source of income, about how long could it cover expenses by borrowing, using savings, selling assets, or seeking help from family or friends. Text: 26% could cover more than six months, 22% less than two weeks, 42% a month or less. atLeast3Months = 26.4 + 18.0 summed by us from the figure labels (labels for each year sum to ~100 and match Table 6).
